## Document-level synthesis

**Source/scope.** CONEVAL, Mexico’s technically and administratively autonomous social-policy evaluator, released this qualitative desk-and-field process evaluation on 20 September 2022 (pp. 1–2, 5). It assesses *Sembrando Vida’s* operation, not impacts, corruption, fiscal incidence, or long-run economic performance; reported scale is program data rather than independently validated outcomes.

**Relevant findings (5B.1, 5B.6–5B.9).** *Sembrando Vida* formally targets residents of socially deprived municipalities with MXN 5,000 monthly, inputs, and continuing technical support to establish 2.5 hectares of agroforestry and meet basic food needs. Official 2021 figures claimed 450,099 participants in 21 states, 1,089,210 hectares reforested, and 743 million trees planted—62% of target (p. 2). CONEVAL observed clear selection rules and monthly register updates, supporting rule-based targeting, and meaningful female participation with gender equity and rotation in local farming-learning communities (pp. 2, 4); it did not establish distributive incidence or final welfare or environmental gains.

CONEVAL found permanent technical accompaniment valuable and local “Distrito CAC” groups capable of solving problems, including delaying transplantation and tending deficient plants to improve survival (pp. 3–4). Contrary evidence showed weak implementation capacity: territorial staff had limited input into production targets, planting density, and crop systems, causing plan revisions and creating water-demand and local-suitability risks; local input shortages, inadequate storage/distribution infrastructure, and technically deficient Defence Secretariat plants shifted costs to technicians or beneficiaries and endangered survival; limited or malfunctioning Banco del Bienestar facilities obstructed payments; and most post-2019 communities lacked the three prescribed youth trainees needed for monitoring (pp. 3–4).

The administration permitted autonomous public evaluation, and the S-Núcleo system supported detailed daily monitoring. Yet technicians reported burdensome data entry, while the results framework lacked indicators for social outcomes and even “food sufficiency,” an explicit objective; CONEVAL recommended remedies, but this release provides no evidence they were adopted or that reported outputs were validated (p. 4). During COVID-19, meetings and training were suspended temporarily and delivery, monitoring, and calendars reorganized, slowing implementation; the document does not evaluate the response’s funding, targeting transparency, or later correction (p. 5).

**Limits.** The document supports a mixed process finding: a formally poverty-targeted, technically supported program with rule-based enrollment and useful local adaptation, but serious planning, input-quality, infrastructure, payment, staffing, and outcome-measurement deficiencies. It cannot determine whether the program generated sustainable prosperity rather than popularity or patronage, nor answer 5B.2–5B.5 or 5B.10.
